implementation_notes: There is no API here; this is a structural measurement and a refactoring. The measurement that works is the internal usage map: for each field, list the methods that touch it, and for each method, list the fields it touches. Clusters of co-touched fields and methods are the candidate classes — the same technique the Siemens god-class work uses, and it is more reliable than splitting by field name or by subject matter. Then Extract Class per cluster, fields and methods together, one per commit. The published threshold is a useful trigger rather than a rule: 60 or more attributes and operations on one class indicates a blob, but a record type, a generated binding or a wire struct has many fields and no behaviour and is not one.
idiom_name: Extract Class: group fields with the methods that read and write them
code_sketch:
# the measurement: internal usage map, not field names
field -> { render, validate, toRow }        # cluster 1
field -> { connect, retry, shutdown }        # cluster 2
# blob: Controller { 18 fields, 60+ methods, both clusters in one class
# after Extract Class: Renderer{...} / Connection{...} / Controller{...}
pitfalls: Splitting on field count alone produces a class explosion with one field per class.
Extracting fields without their methods leaves a data bag beside a god service.
A `Common` object holding the fields every cluster touched recreates the coupling under a new name.
Record types, generated bindings and framework entities have many fields and no behaviour — classify before you split.
